title: SpecForge: Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents via Behavioral Specifications

paper.title: SpecForge: Recursive Self-Improvement for Coding Agents via Behavioral Specifications
paper.abstract:
Abstract Coding agents based on frozen language models can improve their
performance by refining the external context they rely on, without
updating model weights. In this paper, we study recursive
self-improvement (RSI) through behavioral specifications :
natural-language code documentation that describes the behavior of
program entities and guides agents in generating correct code.
We formulate a self-improvement loop in which an agent generates
code from its current specifications, evaluates the generated code
using execution-verified tests, and refines the specifications
based on observed failures. The improved specifications then guide
subsequent code generation, allowing the agent to progressively
improve its understanding of the codebase.
However, recursive refinement is challenging because program
entities are interdependent. Improving the specification of one
entity can inadvertently degrade the correctness of others,
a phenomenon we call output coupling . This creates a whack-a-mole effect in which local improvements cause
regressions elsewhere, preventing consistent progress.
We introduce SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search
framework that addresses this challenge through three mechanisms:
(i) Pareto-guided state selection preserves complementary
specification states and prevents premature commitment;
(ii) dependency-constrained entity selection prioritizes
callee-before-caller refinement; and (iii) error-diversified
expansion explores multiple refinements using different subsets
of test failures.
On DevEval+ , SpecForge achieves the best performance
across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with
Claude-4.5-Sonnet and a 5.7-percentage-point average improvement
over the strongest baseline.
The improved specifications also make the agent better at tasks outside the loop: they transfer to cross-language translation and to new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents.
The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/SpecForge .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models are increasingly used as autonomous coding agents. Systems such as Cursor [ 1 ] , Codex [ 2 ] , and Claude Code [ 3 ] can generate code, implement new features, and modify existing software with limited human intervention. Their effectiveness, however, depends heavily on how well they understand the behavior of the codebase they work with. This understanding is essential for tasks such as repository-level code generation [ 4 , 5 ] , legacy system migration [ 6 ] , cross-language reimplementation [ 7 , 8 ] , and new-feature implementation [ 9 ] . One way to provide such understanding is through behavioral specifications : natural-language code documentation that describes what individual program entities (e.g., functions, classes, and methods) do, including their inputs, outputs, and important behavioral constraints. Unlike traditional documentation intended primarily for human readers, these specifications serve as actionable knowledge that coding agents can use to generate and modify code. Importantly, because specifications are expressed in natural language, agents can also revise them based on feedback, creating an opportunity for self-improvement without changing the underlying language model. This motivates specification-mediated recursive self-improvement (RSI) , in which a coding agent iteratively improves its own behavioral specifications using feedback from code generation and execution, without modifying the underlying model weights. Starting from initial specifications, the agent generates code conditioned on these specifications alone and evaluates the generated implementations through unit tests. Test failures reveal missing or ambiguous behavioral information, which the agent uses to refine the specifications. The refined specifications then guide the next round of code generation, forming a recursive self-improvement loop. In our setting, the tests are automatically generated from the reference implementation and validated through execution, retaining only tests that pass. This provides reliable, execution-grounded feedback without requiring human annotations. Importantly, the objective is not to improve the reconstructed code itself, but to produce more accurate behavioral specifications. Their quality is measured not by readability or similarity to human-written documentation [ 10 , 11 ] , but by whether an agent can reconstruct behaviorally correct code from them. The resulting specifications capture reusable knowledge of the existing codebase, which can support downstream tasks such as cross-language translation and new-feature implementation, even when no reference implementation of the desired output is available. Despite its promise, specification-based RSI faces a fundamental challenge: program entities are not independent . Existing language-space optimization methods, such as MIPROv2 [ 12 ] , GEPA [ 13 ] , and ACE [ 14 ] , demonstrate that language models can improve their own context through iterative refinement and feedback [ 15 , 16 ] . However, directly applying this approach to behavioral specifications is difficult because changes to one entity can affect the behavior of others. We refer to this phenomenon as output coupling . It arises in two ways. First, dependency coupling occurs when the correctness of a caller depends on the behavior of its callees. Refining a caller before its callees are correctly specified can therefore produce misleading feedback. Second, generation coupling occurs because a coding model may condition on the entire specification bundle, so modifying one specification can change how other entities are generated, even without direct dependencies. Consequently, an update that fixes one entity may break another, creating a whack-a-mole effect: improvements are repeatedly undone by subsequent refinements, and the optimization process may oscillate rather than converge. For recursive self-improvement to be effective, it must therefore address three requirements: preserving previous progress, respecting dependencies between entities, and handling noisy or incomplete feedback during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework for recursive self-improvement through behavioral specifications. Instead of following a single sequence of specification revisions, SpecForge explores multiple candidate specification states through three complementary mechanisms: ❶ Where to search: Pareto-guided state selection maintains an archive of non-dominated specification states with complementary strengths across program entities. This preserves alternative refinement paths and prevents premature commitment to a single solution. ❷ What to refine: Dependency-constrained entity selection uses the program’s call graph to restrict refinement to entities whose callees have already been resolved. A discounted-UCB bandit then adaptively allocates the refinement budget among eligible entities. ❸ How to refine: Error-diversified expansion generates multiple refinement candidates from different subsets of failing tests, allowing the search to explore alternative explanations for observed failures and reducing sensitivity to noisy feedback. Together, these mechanisms mitigate refinement interference and enable improvements to accumulate across recursive iterations. We evaluate SpecForge on DevEval+ , where behavioral specification quality is measured by the correctness of code reconstructed from the generated specifications. Across five backbone language models, SpecForge consistently outperforms strong documentation, prompt-optimization, and coding-agent baselines. In particular, it achieves a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and improves over the strongest baseline by 5.7 percentage points on average. We further evaluate whether the optimized specifications remain useful beyond the original code-generation task. Results on cross-language translation and new-feature implementation show that these specifications provide reusable behavioral knowledge that improves coding-agent performance in different software engineering settings. These findings suggest that refining behavioral specifications provides a practical approach to recursive self-improvement for coding agents, without requiring model weight updates. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We study specification-mediated recursive self-improvement for coding agents, in which behavioral specifications are iteratively improved through code generation and execution feedback. We identify output coupling as a central challenge that prevents naive iterative refinement from accumulating progress. • We introduce SpecForge , a dependency-guided multi-frontier tree search framework that combines Pareto-guided state selection, dependency-constrained entity selection, and error-diversified expansion to mitigate refinement interference and enable cumulative specification improvement. • We demonstrate that SpecForge consistently outperforms strong baselines on DevEval+ across five backbone models, and that its optimized specifications improve downstream cross-language translation and new-feature implementation.

sections.heading: 2 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We study behavioral specification optimization : given source code, the goal is to produce, for every program entity, a natural-language specification from which a code-generation model can reconstruct a correct implementation without seeing the code. sections.heading: Output Coupling.
sections.text: The central challenge is that program entities cannot be optimized independently. First, dependency coupling arises because if e i e_{i} calls e j e_{j} , then the correctness of c i c_{i} depends on the realized behavior of c j c_{j} . Second, generation coupling arises because the code generator conditions on the full specification bundle 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , so changing d j d_{j} may alter the generated code for e i e_{i} even without a direct call edge. Together, these effects produce a whack-a-mole phenomenon: refining the specification of one entity may improve that entity while destabilizing others. Formal definitions are deferred to Appendix § A .

sections.heading: Search Formulation.
sections.text: The optimization is difficult because specification quality is only observable after code generation and execution. This makes behavioral specification optimization a structured search problem over specification states. Different partial solutions resolve different subsets of entities, and these resolved subsets determine which subsequent refinements are meaningful under dependency constraints. Figure 1 : Search tree view of behavioral specification optimization. Each node is a specification state. Different states solve different subsets of entities and therefore expose different eligible next refinements. Rather than committing to a single rewrite trajectory, our solution preserves multiple competitive frontiers and expands them selectively.

sections.heading: 3 Proposed Method
sections.text: We propose SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework for behavioral specification optimization. SpecForge instantiates the self-improvement loop of § 1 as search: each node is a specification state evaluated by executing the code generated from it, each edge is one self-revision driven by the failures of that code, and every revision starts from a state that earlier revisions produced. Figure 1 illustrates the search process: specification optimization proceeds not as a single rewrite trajectory, but as search over multiple partial solutions with different future refinement opportunities. By managing this search so that local refinements accumulate into stable global progress, SpecForge directly targets the whack-a-mole behavior induced by output coupling.

sections.heading: State Representation.
sections.text: SpecForge organizes optimization as tree search over specification states. A node is v = ( 𝒟 v , ϕ v , 𝒮 v ) v=(\mathcal{D}_{v},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{v},\mathcal{S}_{v}) , where 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{v} is the current specification bundle, ϕ v ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] n \boldsymbol{\phi}_{v}\in[0,1]^{n} is the per-entity pass-rate vector, and 𝒮 v \mathcal{S}_{v} is the set of resolved entities. An edge v → 𝑒 v ′ v\xrightarrow{e}v^{\prime} denotes refining exactly one entity e e : d e ′ ∼ P θ ( ⋅ ∣ d e , ℱ e ( v ) ) , d i ′ = d i ∀ i ≠ e , d^{\prime}_{e}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid d_{e},\mathcal{F}_{e}(v)),\qquad d^{\prime}_{i}=d_{i}\;\;\forall i\neq e, (1) where ℱ e ​ ( v ) \mathcal{F}_{e}(v) denotes the failure feedback for entity e e at state v v . This single-entity transition is the basic search step in SpecForge : it keeps refinements localized, makes feedback easier to attribute, and allows the method to explore multiple competing partial solutions in parallel.

sections.heading: Multi-Frontier Tree Search.
sections.text: Starting from a root node v 0 v_{0} corresponding to the initial specifications, SpecForge maintains a Pareto archive 𝒜 \mathcal{A} of non-dominated states (initialized as { v 0 } \{v_{0}\} ) together with a shared entity-selection bandit. Each iteration resolves three coupled decisions: where to search (§ 3.1 ), what to refine (§ 3.2 ), and how to refine (§ 3.3 ). Concretely, the iteration (i) samples a parent node v v from 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ; (ii) selects an eligible entity e e to refine via a discounted-UCB policy over per-entity gap-closing rates; and (iii) expands v v into W W children, each obtained by substituting a refined specification d e ′ d^{\prime}_{e} into 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{v} , regenerating the code of the full module from the updated specifications, and re-evaluating the full test suite to produce ϕ v ′ \boldsymbol{\phi}_{v^{\prime}} . The W W children are then folded back into both upper levels: non-dominated children enter 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , introducing new frontier diversity for future state selection, and the best child’s Δ ​ ϕ e \Delta\phi_{e} updates the bandit for future entity selection. Once B B iterations, SpecForge returns the specification bundle 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{v} achieving the largest | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| over all visited states. Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 summarize the procedure. Figure 2 : Overview of SpecForge . Each iteration resolves three decisions: where to search, what to refine, and how to refine. ❶ Pareto-guided state selection samples from an archive of non-dominated specification states with complementary strengths. ❷ Dependency-constrained entity selection only refines entities whose callees are already solved. ❸ Error-diversified expansion generates multiple children from different subsets of failing tests. Strong children are fed back into both the archive and the entity-selection policy.

sections.heading: 3.1 Pareto-Guided State Selection
sections.text: The first step is to decide where to search next, i.e., which previously visited state to expand. Because improving one entity may degrade another, scalar ranking is often too coarse. We therefore maintain an archive 𝒜 \mathcal{A} of non-dominated states under coordinate-wise dominance over pass-rate vectors: ϕ v ′ ⪰ ϕ v ⟺ ϕ i ( 𝒟 v ′ ) ≥ ϕ i ( 𝒟 v ) for all i . \boldsymbol{\phi}_{v^{\prime}}\succeq\boldsymbol{\phi}_{v}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\phi_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{v^{\prime}})\geq\phi_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{v})\;\;\text{for all }i. (2) A new child enters the archive if no existing state dominates it; any states that it dominates are removed. This archive preserves complementary frontier states . One state may already solve low-level utility entities, while another may have progressed further on higher-level orchestration logic. Crucially, different archive states induce different feasible next refinements because they solve different subsets of entities. Maintaining multiple such states prevents premature commitment to one unstable trajectory and thus helps to escape local optima (refer to § B.1 for detailed analysis).

sections.heading: Frequency-Weighted Sampling.
sections.text: To select which archive node to expand, we sample from the Pareto front of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} (Algorithm 2 ). For each entity e i e_{i} , we identify the archive node(s) attaining the highest ϕ i \phi_{i} and assign credit to those node(s), splitting it evenly in the case of ties. A node’s sampling weight is the total credit it accumulates across entities. This biases expansion toward nodes that are frontier-best on more entity-wise dimensions, thereby preserving complementary search frontiers rather than collapsing prematurely to a single trajectory.

sections.heading: 3.2 Dependency-Constrained Entity Selection

(3) That is, an entity is eligible only if it remains unsolved and all of its callees are already resolved. This enforces a callee-before-caller refinement order and mitigates dependency-induced interference. Recursive calls are handled by contracting each strongly connected component into a jointly refined meta-entity (Appendix C.1 ). When multiple entities are eligible, SpecForge allocates budget adaptively using a discounted UCB policy [ 17 ] . The policy therefore balances uncertainty, past success, and remaining improvement potential.

sections.text: Given a selected state v v and entity e e , the third step expands v v into W W child states, each representing a distinct refinement of d e d_{e} . The key challenge is that failing tests are diagnostically heterogeneous: some directly expose the behavioral detail missing from the specification, while others are redundant, weakly informative, or induced by cascading dependency errors. This is consistent with prior findings that test cases differ substantially in fault-localization value, LLM-generated tests often cluster around similar patterns, and adding more tests can even hurt diagnosis when uninformative cases dilute the signal [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments test the claims behind specification-mediated self-improvement: that improvements accumulate instead of oscillating (§ 4.2 and § 4.3 ), that each component of SpecForge contributes to the stability of the loop (§ 4.4 ), and that the improved specifications make the agent better at tasks outside the loop (§ 4.5 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Benchmark. We evaluate SpecForge on DevEval+ , a benchmark for evaluating behavioral specifications through code reconstruction and execution-based verification across modules with complex inter-entity dependencies. It consists of 20 Python modules , 247 entities , and 760 test cases . The modules are drawn from DevEval [ 5 ] and supplemented with additional GitHub repositories to broaden domain coverage, including finance, biological analysis, and signal processing. DevEval+ is structurally nontrivial, with an average dependency depth of 4.2, making it a suitable testbed for studying output coupling under repository-scale generation (full details in Appendix H ). sections.heading: 4.2 Main Results
sections.text: Table 1 presents comprehensive comparisons across methods and base LLMs (50 rollouts). SpecForge achieves the highest solve rates across all models: 88.9% with Qwen3-235B-A22B, 89.6% with Gemini-2.5-Flash, 90.9% with GPT-4o, 91.0% with Gemini-3.1-Pro, and 94.9% with Claude-4.5-Sonnet. The results reveal a clear hierarchy of failure modes. Static methods (14.5–35.3%) expose a documentation–specification gap : documentation optimized for human readability appears imprecise about behavior to serve as a specification for code-synthesis models, which interpret underspecified phrases literally but resolve ambiguities unpredictably. Monolithic prompt optimizers improve substantially—ACE reaches 62.8% on GPT-4o via its generate-reflect-curate pipeline—but suffer from attribution failure (cannot identify which entity caused a test failure) and coupling amplification (a single rewrite alters all entities simultaneously). Commercial agents with full augmentation (Cursor+Topo+Test: 52.1%, Claude Code+Topo+Test: 61.9% on Claude-4.5-Sonnet) confirm that topological ordering and test feedback are valuable signals, yet both still trail SpecForge by 33.0–42.8%. Iterative refinement with topological ordering reaches 54.3% on GPT-4o but plateaus due to the whack-a-mole phenomenon: without Pareto archiving and diversified exploration, correct ordering alone cannot overcome interference at the same topological level. DocSearch is the strongest baseline (81.5–90.4%) and the only one that optimizes the same objective. It already orders refinement callee-before-caller and diversifies the error context, but it follows a single search path and commits a refinement only if no entity regresses. SpecForge exceeds it on every backbone, by 3.8–7.4 points in solve rate (5.7 on average) and 3.6–6.6 points in pass rate. The margin is largest on the two weakest backbones (7.4 points on both Qwen3-235B-A22B and Gemini-2.5-Flash) and narrows to 3.8–4.5 points on the two strongest, consistent with the role of the Pareto archive: when no candidate passes a no-regression test, a single-path search must abandon the entity, whereas SpecForge can continue from another frontier. The improvement pattern is remarkably consistent across LLMs: despite substantial differences in base capability, SpecForge delivers absolute solve-rate gains of 23.5–49.1 percentage points over the best iterative baseline across all models, consistent with the hypothesis that the method targets a broadly shared structural difficulty. sections.heading: 4.3 Token Budget Efficiency Analysis
sections.text: Figure 3 plots cross-module average pass rate ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} against budget step, evaluated on ground-truth tests at every 10 rollouts. Among entity-wise methods (Figure 3 (a)), Iterative refinement oscillates between 45–54% as random entity selection triggers generation coupling—modifying one entity’s specification perturbs code generation for unrelated entities. Iterative+Topo eliminates the most direct interference by enforcing callee-before-caller order, rising to 57% by B = 20 B{=}20 , but plateaus once all remaining candidates are callers at the same topological level where sibling coupling persists. Among monolithic methods (Figure 3 (b)), MIPROv2 plateaus at 31% by B = 20 B{=}20 as its Bayesian surrogate exhausts the candidate space under single-instance optimization; GEPA peaks at 37% ( B = 20 B{=}20 ) then declines monotonically to 24% because its graph evolution lacks running-best retention, making exploration into worse regions irreversible; ACE reaches the highest monolithic score (64%) but exhibits repeated regressions (e.g., 38 % 38\% to 30 % 30\% between B = 10 B{=}10 and 20 20 ) where each monolithic rewrite simultaneously fixes and breaks entities, recovering only through playbook accumulation of failure-derived rules. SpecForge rises steadily from 41% to 93% across both panels: the steepest gains occur in the first 10 rollouts ( + 29 % +29\% ) as D-UCB exploration combined with topological constraints rapidly solves leaf entities, with diminishing but sustained progress thereafter as the Pareto archive preserves complementary frontier states, converting exploration cost into eventual progress rather than permanent regression.

sections.heading: 4.4 Component Contribution Analysis
sections.text: Figure 4 : (Left) Cross-language translation . Optimized specifications ( + 26.0 % +26.0\% over Source-only) transfer effectively across languages; combining specifications with source code achieves the best results (76.2%). (Right) New-feature implementation on SWE-Dev . SpecForge -generated specifications surpass the default PRD provided by the SWE-Dev benchmark, achieving the highest pass rate on both difficulty levels despite never accessing the PRD or target tests. Figure 3 (c) isolates each component’s contribution. Reverse topological order ( − 18.6 % -18.6\% ) is the structural foundation: without dependency constraints, the search refines callers before their callees are stabilized, allowing interference to propagate through the entire call chain. D-UCB bandit ( − 10.4 % -10.4\% ) demonstrates that adaptive budget allocation is critical: its gap-closing rate estimate θ ^ e \hat{\theta}_{e} learns entity-level repairability and directs budget accordingly. Error diversity ( − 9.5 % -9.5\% ) addresses exploration collapse: diversified batch sampling increases the probability of encountering informative error combinations (Appendix § D ). Pareto archive ( − 5.2 % -5.2\% ) preserves frontier diversity, enabling recovery from suboptimal early refinements; its value increases on harder modules with deeper dependency chains.

sections.heading: 4.5 Downstream Utility of Optimized Specifications
sections.text: We evaluate whether SpecForge -optimized specifications transfer beyond the original code-generation setting through two downstream tasks: cross-language translation (§ 4.5.1 ) and new-feature implementation (§ 4.5.2 ). Both tasks compare the outputs of four methods from the main evaluation—RepoAgent, Claude Code ∗ 2 2 2 Claude Code ∗ denotes the +Topo+Test configuration running on Claude-4.5-Sonnet, as Claude Code does not support GPT-4o. , ACE, and SpecForge —with GPT-4o as the code-generation backbone.

sections.heading: 4.5.1 Cross-Language Translation
sections.text: Experimental Setup. We evaluate cross-language transfer on DevEval+-Java , a JUnit 5 test harness covering a 16-module subset of DevEval+ (208 entities, 680 test cases). We exclude modules whose Python implementations depend on libraries without direct Java equivalents. Each harness mirrors the original Python tests, preserving input data and expected outputs to ensure semantic equivalence (Appendix H.6 ). We evaluate Source-only translation (Python source → \to Java, no specification) alongside the four methods above. For SpecForge we additionally test a Spec+Source variant that provides both the specification and the source code. Results and Analysis. Figure 4 (left) reports both solve rate | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| and pass rate ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} for each condition. Source-only translation achieves 39.7 % 39.7\% / 50.5 % 50.5\% ( | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| / ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} ), while static documentation (RepoAgent, 33.5 % 33.5\% / 44.6 % 44.6\% ) performs worse on both metrics—imprecise human-oriented descriptions introduce ambiguities absent from source code. Performance improves steadily with optimization sophistication: Claude Code ∗ ( 45.9 % 45.9\% / 53.1 % 53.1\% ), ACE ( 49.7 % 49.7\% / 56.0 % 56.0\% ), and SpecForge ( 65.7 % 65.7\% / 71.3 % 71.3\% , + 26.0 % +26.0\% solve rate over Source-only). Per-entity optimization produces precise behavioral specifications describing what each function computes rather than how it computes in Python, freeing the LLM to choose Java-appropriate implementations. The Spec+Source combination achieves the best results ( 76.2 % 76.2\% / 80.4 % 80.4\% ), as specifications and source code provide complementary “what” and “how” signals. The quality gradient (static < < commercial < < monolithic < < entity-wise) is preserved across languages, confirming that SpecForge ’s precision reflects higher-quality behavioral specifications.

sections.heading: 4.5.2 New Feature Implementation
sections.text: Whereas cross-language translation evaluates specifications on re-implementing existing code in a different language, real-world development more often requires implementing new functionality atop an existing codebase, with specifications of the existing code as guidance. We therefore evaluate on SWE-Dev [ 9 ] , a benchmark in which an LLM must implement new functions—specified by a Product Requirements Document (PRD)—within real open-source packages, validated against developer-written test suites. Experimental Setup. We select 10 packages from SWE-Dev , comprising 27 feature-implementation instances (15 easy and 12 hard). For each package, we run all four methods on the existing source code to produce behavioral specifications of the current codebase; these specifications are then provided as context when the LLM implements new functions. We compare two conditions, which share the stubbed source and differ only in the accompanying text (Appendix I ): (i) Spec+Source : stubs paired with the signature and docstring of each target function, plus the specifications of the existing codebase produced by each of the four methods; (ii) PRD+Source : stubs paired with the default PRD provided by the SWE-Dev benchmark. We report Pass@1 following SWE-Dev ’s evaluation protocol, broken down by difficulty level. Results and Analysis. Figure 4 (right) reports Pass@1 broken down by difficulty level. Among the four methods, the quality gradient observed in the main evaluation and cross-language experiments persists: RepoAgent (22.0% easy, 14.0% hard), Claude Code* (38.0%, 27.0%), and ACE (50.0%, 38.0%) yield progressively larger improvements, while SpecForge achieves the highest performance (74.5% easy, 51.7% hard), surpassing even the SWE-Dev reference PRD (55.7% easy, 44.6% hard) by +18.8 and +7.1 percentage points, respectively. Appendix I further analyzes why SpecForge outperforms the PRD.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Recursive Self-Improvement. Self-improving LLM systems differ first in the substrate into which an improvement is written. Weight-space methods write into model parameters: the model is fine-tuned on data it generated itself [ 25 , 26 ] , on rewards derived from its own outputs [ 27 ] , or on rewards from a grounded environment [ 28 ] . The gain is amortized across tasks, but it cannot be read, diffed, or reverted. Context-space methods keep the weights frozen and write into the harness instead, through verbal self-refinement [ 29 , 30 , 16 ] , prompt search and textual gradients [ 15 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 12 , 13 ] , experience memory [ 14 ] , skill and tool synthesis [ 34 ] , or search over the whole scaffold [ 35 ] ; at the frontier, the procedure that performs the update is itself rewritten [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] . The improvement signal ranges from the model’s own judgment [ 39 , 40 ] to external verifiers such as tests [ 41 , 42 , 43 ] , compilers [ 44 , 45 ] , and environments [ 34 , 46 ] . SpecForge is a context-space method with an execution-based improvement signal and a fixed update procedure. The key difficulty in such a recursive self-improvement loop is that behavioral specifications are inherently coupled through the code generated from them, so that an improvement to one can cause a global regression and make the iterative process oscillate. Coding Agents. Coding is among the most rapidly advancing capabilities of LLM agents, in large part because code is executable, verifiable, and searchable: a candidate can be run, checked against tests, and improved by search. Agents such as Cursor, Codex, and Claude Code [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] now resolve issues and implement features across entire repositories [ 47 , 48 , 4 , 5 , 9 ] . The same property is carrying agents beyond conventional software, wherever the artifact can be expressed as a program or other interpretable text: games [ 49 ] , explanatory videos rendered from animation code [ 50 , 51 ] , 3D scenes written as Blender scripts [ 52 ] , and symbolic music [ 53 ] . SpecForge is complementary to these agents: it supplies behavioral specifications that a coding agent can condition on, which in our experiments improve cross-language translation and new-feature implementation (§ 4.5 ). Code Documentation. Documentation generation has evolved from template-based heuristics [ 54 , 55 , 56 ] through neural summarization [ 57 , 58 ] to modern LLM-based repository-level approaches. RepoAgent [ 10 ] extracts structural patterns from repositories to generate API references with hierarchical organization, while DocAgent [ 11 ] employs retrieval-augmented generation to produce context-aware explanations grounded in relevant code snippets. Both optimize for subjective quality metrics—clarity, completeness, and helpfulness—evaluated through human assessment or proxy metrics like BLEU scores against reference documentation. These approaches uniformly assume documentation serves human developers and measure quality through readability heuristics rather than downstream task performance. See Appendix K for further related work.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework that makes specification-mediated self-improvement stable and compounding. A frozen coding agent improves by rewriting the behavioral specifications in its harness from the failures of the code it writes from them; unlike documentation written for human readers, a specification is judged only through the code it induces. Within this formulation, the central challenge is output coupling : because generated entities are behaviorally interdependent, locally beneficial refinements can trigger global regressions, rendering standard monolithic or sequential refinement unstable. SpecForge addresses this challenge through Pareto-guided frontier preservation, dependency-constrained entity selection, and error-diversified expansion, enabling stable progress under coupled search dynamics. Empirically, it consistently outperforms strong baselines on DevEval+ , exhibits superior search efficiency and robustness, and produces specifications that improve downstream performance in both cross-language translation and new-feature implementation, indicating that what the loop improves is reusable knowledge of the codebase rather than a fit to the tests that guided it.

sections.heading: Appendix B Theoretical Analysis
sections.text: This section provides theoretical analysis and complete proofs for the theoretical results stated in the main paper.

sections.heading: B.1 Why Multi-Frontier Search Escapes Certain Frontier-Local Optima
sections.text: A central role of the Pareto archive in SpecForge is to prevent the search from collapsing onto a single refinement trajectory too early. We formalize this benefit through the notion of frontier-local optimality : a state may be locally saturated with respect to its currently eligible refinements, while another non-dominated state still exposes a different eligibility frontier from which progress remains possible. Definition 4 (Frontier-Local Optimum) . Let v = ( 𝒟 v , ϕ v , 𝒮 v ) v=(\mathcal{D}_{v},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{v},\mathcal{S}_{v}) be a search state with eligibility frontier ℰ elig ​ ( v ) \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{elig}}(v) . We say that v v is a frontier-local optimum if for every eligible entity e ∈ ℰ elig ​ ( v ) e\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{elig}}(v) and every admissible single-entity refinement v → 𝑒 v ′ v\xrightarrow{e}v^{\prime} , | 𝒮 v ′ | ≤ | 𝒮 v | . |\mathcal{S}_{v^{\prime}}|\leq|\mathcal{S}_{v}|. (8) That is, no refinement available from the current frontier increases the solved-set objective. This notion captures the practical failure mode of single-path refinement: once the current state becomes frontier-locally optimal, all subsequent search effort is confined to a neighborhood with no objective improvement. The key observation is that frontier-local optimality is state-dependent : because eligibility depends on the solved set 𝒮 v \mathcal{S}_{v} , two states with similar objective values may expose different feasible next refinements. Definition 5 (Archive Dominance) . For two states u u and v v , we say that u u dominates v v if ϕ u ⪰ ϕ v ⟺ ϕ i ( 𝒟 u ) ≥ ϕ i ( 𝒟 v ) for all i ∈ [ n ] . \boldsymbol{\phi}_{u}\succeq\boldsymbol{\phi}_{v}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\phi_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{u})\geq\phi_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{v})\;\;\text{for all }i\in[n]. (9) A Pareto archive 𝒜 \mathcal{A} contains only non-dominated states. The importance of this criterion is that it preserves states with complementary strengths across entities rather than only the current best state under a scalar score. Such states can induce different solved sets and therefore different eligibility frontiers. Assumption 1 (Complementary Frontier Reachability) . Suppose there exist two non-dominated states u u and v v in the search tree such that: 1. u u is a frontier-local optimum; 2. there exists an entity e ⋆ ∈ ℰ elig ​ ( v ) ∖ ℰ elig ​ ( u ) e^{\star}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{elig}}(v)\setminus\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{elig}}(u) and a refinement v → e ⋆ v ⋆ v\xrightarrow{e^{\star}}v^{\star} such that | 𝒮 v ⋆ | > | 𝒮 v | |\mathcal{S}_{v^{\star}}|>|\mathcal{S}_{v}| . This assumption states that one archived frontier may be saturated while another still contains a productive move. It is natural in our setting because eligibility is induced by the solved subset, and different trajectories typically solve different subsets of entities. Proposition 1 (Multi-Frontier Advantage) . Under Assumption 1 , any search strategy restricted to expanding only the single incumbent state u u cannot improve the objective | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| , whereas a multi-frontier strategy that retains both u u and v v in a Pareto archive has nonzero probability of reaching a state with strictly larger solved set. Proof. Since u u is frontier-locally optimal, by Definition 4 , every admissible refinement from u u satisfies | 𝒮 u ′ | ≤ | 𝒮 u | |\mathcal{S}_{u^{\prime}}|\leq|\mathcal{S}_{u}| . Hence any single-path strategy confined to descendants of u u cannot obtain an immediate objective improvement. By Assumption 1 , there exists another archived state v v and an eligible entity e ⋆ ∈ ℰ elig ​ ( v ) e^{\star}\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{elig}}(v) such that refining e ⋆ e^{\star} yields a child v ⋆ v^{\star} with | 𝒮 v ⋆ | > | 𝒮 v | |\mathcal{S}_{v^{\star}}|>|\mathcal{S}_{v}| . Because u u and v v are non-dominated, a Pareto archive retains both states. Therefore, any archive-sampling policy that assigns nonzero probability to every archived state has nonzero probability of selecting v v and then refining e ⋆ e^{\star} , reaching an improved state. Thus, retaining multiple non-dominated frontiers strictly enlarges the set of reachable improving moves compared with single-path search. ∎ Proposition 1 formalizes the role of the Pareto archive in escaping local optima. Its benefit is not merely diversity for its own sake; rather, archive diversity induces frontier diversity . Because eligibility is determined by the solved subset, preserving multiple non-dominated states preserves multiple feasible continuation sets. When one frontier is exhausted, another may still expose an improving refinement. The argument also clarifies why scalar best-first retention is brittle in our setting. A state with the highest current | 𝒮 | |\mathcal{S}| or ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} need not be the most promising continuation state if its eligibility frontier is already saturated. By preserving non-dominated states with complementary per-entity strengths, the Pareto archive acts as a structural hedge against premature convergence.

sections.heading: Implication for SpecForge .
sections.text: In SpecForge , multi-frontier search is realized by maintaining a Pareto archive over per-entity pass-rate vectors and sampling from it during expansion. This design ensures that the search does not over-commit to a single locally attractive trajectory, but can continue from alternative archived frontiers whose dependency structure admits further progress.

sections.heading: Empirical Motivation.
sections.text: Our theoretical treatment is motivated by two recurring empirical observations from the software engineering literature. 1. Failing tests differ substantially in diagnostic value. Not all failures are equally informative for identifying the underlying defect. Some tests reveal the root cause directly, whereas others fail only through cascading effects or repeatedly exercise the same execution path. In the context of LLM-generated tests, Yuan et al. [ 18 ] observe that generated inputs often cluster around similar patterns, leaving critical edge cases underexplored and further increasing heterogeneity in diagnostic usefulness. 2. Using more tests can degrade diagnosis rather than improve it. Prior work on fault localization shows that adding tests beyond a certain point may reduce localization quality when additional tests contribute little new information. Chen et al. [ 19 ] show that excessive or low-value tests can dilute diagnostic signals, while Su et al. [ 20 ] demonstrate that carefully selected subsets can outperform the full test suite for fault localization. In our setting, these observations imply that the full failure set may contain substantial noise. We attribute noisy errors ℱ − \mathcal{F}^{-} to three common sources: (i) cascading failures , where a test fails because a callee is incorrectly implemented rather than because the target entity’s specification is inadequate; (ii) redundant signals , where multiple tests expose essentially the same failure mode and therefore add little incremental information; and (iii) misleading co-occurrence , where presenting several errors together encourages the optimizer LLM to infer spurious patterns that are not causally related to the true knowledge gap. Remark 1 (Connection to Fault Localization) . Our result formalizes a central intuition from fault localization: for diagnosis, test quality often matters more than test quantity [ 20 ] . Diversified error-batch sampling can be viewed as a hedging strategy: by exploring multiple subsets of the failure set, it increases the chance of encountering a batch dominated by informative signals, without requiring prior knowledge of the latent partition between informative and noisy errors.

sections.heading: Appendix C Algorithm Details
C.1 Recursive and Cyclic Call Graphs
sections.text: The eligibility frontier (Eq. ( 3 )) requires every callee of an entity to be resolved before the entity can be refined. On a call graph with cycles this condition can never hold for the entities on a cycle, so SpecForge removes cycles before search.

sections.heading: Self-recursion.
sections.text: A self-call ( e , e ) ∈ E (e,e)\in E is ignored when evaluating eligibility: an entity cannot wait for itself to be resolved, and its recursive behavior is described within its own specification d e d_{e} .

sections.heading: Mutual recursion.
sections.text: We compute the strongly connected components (SCCs) of G G and contract each SCC with more than one member into a single meta-entity . The search then operates on refinement units , each of which is either a single entity or a meta-entity. The condensation of G G over these units is a DAG by construction, so the callee-before-caller order and the eligibility gate apply unchanged: a unit is eligible once it is unsolved and all units it calls are resolved, and a meta-entity counts as resolved once all of its members are solved.

sections.heading: Joint refinement of a meta-entity.
sections.text: When a meta-entity is selected, its members are refined together in a single expansion. The refinement prompt presents the source code and current specifications of all members, states that they are mutually recursive, and requires a complete replacement specification for every member, so that the specifications of the cycle remain consistent with one another. The resulting specifications are substituted into 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{v} together, and the child is evaluated as for any other expansion.

sections.text: We use beam width W = 3 W=3 throughout all experiments, balancing the hedging benefit of diversified expansion (Theorem 2 ) against per-iteration cost. Given failing tests ℱ e ​ ( v ) \mathcal{F}_{e}(v) for entity e e at state v v , we sample W W batches independently: each batch 𝐞 k \mathbf{e}_{k} is drawn by selecting ⌈ | ℱ e ​ ( v ) | / 2 ⌉ \lceil|\mathcal{F}_{e}(v)|/2\rceil failures uniformly at random without replacement from ℱ e ​ ( v ) \mathcal{F}_{e}(v) , with batches generated sequentially and any duplicate redrawn until W W distinct batches are obtained. sections.heading: Diagnosis-Prescription Process.
sections.text: Each refinement follows a two-stage process. In the diagnosis stage, the LLM analyzes the error batch to identify the knowledge gap: what information is missing or ambiguous in the current specification that caused the incorrect generation. In the prescription stage, the LLM produces a targeted specification update addressing the diagnosed gap. This decomposition prevents the LLM from making unfocused edits and ensures each refinement is traceable to a specific failure signal. Prompt templates for both stages are provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: D.1 Iterative Refinement: Diagnosis Without Action
sections.text: The Iterative column reveals a striking pattern: the LLM correctly diagnoses the root cause of failure but lacks the mechanism to act on its diagnosis . sections.heading: D.2 ACE: Regression and Recovery Tax
sections.text: ACE’s global playbook mechanism exhibits a different but equally costly failure mode. Its rules accumulate helpful counts across iterations (e.g., [misc-00001] helpful=0 at B = 10 B{=}10 rising to helpful=7 by B = 50 B{=}50 ), and each iteration rewrites all entity specifications simultaneously from the updated playbook. This monolithic approach has no mechanism to protect previously solved entities. The critical event occurs at B = 30 B{=}30 : a global rewrite causes regression from ϕ = 0.670 \phi{=}0.670 to ϕ = 0.604 \phi{=}0.604 , a drop of − 0.066 -0.066 . The reflection diagnoses the failure accurately—“the documentation focused on high-level descriptions and omitted critical details about method behavior”—but this diagnosis applies equally to the entities that were already working . Because ACE rewrites all specifications from the playbook rather than preserving solved entities, the rewrite breaks previously correct descriptions of PnF.get_state and LineBreak.get_ohlc_data , which regress from ϕ e = 100 % \phi_{e}{=}100\% to ϕ e = 50 % \phi_{e}{=}50\% and ϕ e = 75 % \phi_{e}{=}75\% respectively. The next two budget steps ( B = 40 B{=}40 , B = 50 B{=}50 ) are spent recovering from this regression rather than making new progress. By B = 40 B{=}40 , ACE recovers to ϕ = 0.689 \phi{=}0.689 , only marginally above its pre-regression score of 0.670 0.670 at B = 20 B{=}20 , and by B = 50 B{=}50 it reaches ϕ = 0.717 \phi{=}0.717 , a net gain of only + 0.047 +0.047 over three budget steps. Meanwhile, both Renko entities remain at or near zero throughout all 10 iterations, because the global rules are too coarse to capture the entity-specific algorithmic details (e.g., brick initialization alignment, reversal threshold logic) that these methods require. The [misc-00004] rule (“explain how key parameters influence method behavior”) stays frozen at helpful=2 from B = 20 B{=}20 onward, confirming that parameter-specific behavioral descriptions are the hardest to capture at the playbook level.

sections.heading: D.3 SpecForge: Callee-Before-Caller Unlocking
sections.text: SpecForge ’s trajectory illustrates how dependency-guided search converts the same budget into monotonic progress. At B = 10 B{=}10 , the D-UCB bandit selects LineBreak.get_ohlc_data —a leaf entity with no unsolved callees—and solves it in a single step ( ϕ e \phi_{e} : 50 % → 100 % 50\%{\to}100\% ). At B = 20 B{=}20 , the Pareto archive retains this state but finds no eligible entity that improves the frontier, so the module score holds at ϕ = 0.679 \phi{=}0.679 . Crucially, no budget is wasted : the archive simply records that the current state is locally optimal and explores alternative branches. The critical breakthrough comes at B = 30 − 40 B{=}30{-}40 . At B = 30 B{=}30 , the search targets Renko.price_movement_bricks , whose test failure ( assert 63 == 94 ) reveals a brick-count mismatch. The reflection identifies the precise algorithmic gap: “the first brick must align the close price with brick_size to compute first_open .” This targeted, entity-specific diagnosis—impossible under ACE’s global playbook—raises ϕ e \phi_{e} from 0 % 0\% to 50 % 50\% . At B = 40 B{=}40 , the dependency constraint makes PnF.get_ohlc_data eligible (its callee dependencies are resolved). The reflection pinpoints the initialization formula: “ first_open = roundit(first_value, box_size) - box_size .” Solving this callee ( ϕ e \phi_{e} : 0 % → 100 % 0\%{\to}100\% ) triggers a cascade : its caller PnF.get_bar_ohlc_data simultaneously jumps from 33 % 33\% to 100 % 100\% without any modification to its own specification . This is the “callee solved → \to caller unlocked” effect that dependency-constrained search is designed to produce, and that Iterative refinement structurally cannot achieve. By B = 50 B{=}50 , the Pareto archive allocates remaining budget to Renko.period_close_bricks ( ϕ e \phi_{e} : 20 % → 100 % 20\%{\to}100\% ), and the module reaches ϕ = 0.906 \phi{=}0.906 . The radar chart at B = 50 B{=}50 shows the SpecForge polygon (green) nearly filling the entire chart, while Iterative (blue) remains frozen at its B = 20 B{=}20 shape.

sections.heading: D.4 Key Takeaways
sections.text: This module-level trace exposes three failure modes and their structural causes: 1. Dependency blindness (Iterative). The LLM’s reflection is a powerful diagnostic tool—it correctly identifies cross-entity dependencies as the root cause of failure. But without a mechanism to act on dependency structure, this diagnostic power is wasted. The cycling pattern (same entity targeted 3 times, same diagnosis, same ϕ e = 0 % \phi_{e}{=}0\% ) is a direct consequence of treating entities as independent. 2. Collateral damage (ACE). Global rewriting treats the specification bundle as a monolithic artifact, making it impossible to improve one entity without risking others. The regression at B = 30 B{=}30 and subsequent two-step recovery illustrate the “two steps forward, one step back” dynamic that caps ACE’s effective progress rate. Even at convergence ( B = 50 B{=}50 , ϕ = 0.717 \phi{=}0.717 ), entity-specific algorithmic details remain beyond the reach of global rules. 3. Structural unlocking ( SpecForge ). By constraining refinement to entities whose callees are already solved, SpecForge converts callee improvements into free caller improvements. The B = 40 B{=}40 cascade—where solving PnF.get_ohlc_data simultaneously unlocks PnF.get_bar_ohlc_data —demonstrates that dependency-aware search does not merely avoid interference but actively exploits coupling as a source of compounding returns.

sections.heading: Appendix E Fidelity of the Self-Generated Improvement Signal
sections.text: A recursive self-improvement loop is only as sound as the signal that drives it. In SpecForge the loop is fully self-supervised: the agent synthesizes the tests that score its own specifications, and no external label enters the loop. This raises a question that the main results cannot settle on their own, because every method in Table 1 is evaluated on hidden ground-truth tests but optimized against self-generated ones: does the self-generated signal track true behavioral correctness, or does the search merely learn to satisfy its own tests? In the latter case the measured gains would constitute reward hacking rather than self-improvement. Two properties are therefore required of the signal. Fidelity : optimizing against the self-generated signal must yield essentially the same outcome as optimizing against the ground truth. Grounding : the signal must be derived from execution rather than from the model’s own judgment, since Theorem 1 shows that a corrupted signal degrades refinement quality monotonically. This section verifies both properties and characterizes how performance degrades as the signal is weakened.

sections.heading: Construction of the signal.
sections.text: Test oracles are obtained by executing LLM-proposed inputs on the reference implementation to derive the expected outputs (§ J ); output correctness is therefore guaranteed by construction. The only residual imperfection lies in input quality: some generated inputs may be redundant, exercise overlapping code paths, or fail to cover critical edge cases. Error-diversified expansion (§ 3.3 ) is designed for precisely this kind of imperfection: by conditioning each child on a different subset of failing tests rather than on the full test set, it bounds the influence of any individual weak or redundant test.

sections.heading: Experimental design.
sections.text: We hold the search procedure, budget, and backbone (GPT-4o) fixed and vary only the improvement signal (Table 2 ). (i) Signal source : the LLM-generated tests are replaced by the hidden ground-truth tests, an oracle that is unavailable in practice and serves as an upper bound on signal quality. (ii) Signal grounding : execution feedback is replaced by an LLM-as-a-judge score of the generated code against the specification, i.e., the model evaluates itself without executing anything. (iii) Signal coverage : the coverage threshold τ cov \tau_{\mathrm{cov}} used during test generation is lowered from its default of 0.9 (§ J ) to 0.7, 0.5, and 0.3, so that the search is driven by progressively fewer tests.

sections.heading: Fidelity: self-generated vs. ground-truth tests.
sections.text: Replacing LLM-generated tests with ground-truth tests improves ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} only marginally, from 93.2 to 94.8, corresponding to a gain of just 1.6 percentage points. The self-generated signal is thus near-equivalent to the ground truth as an optimization target: the loop does not exploit its own tests, and the improvements reported in Table 1 reflect genuinely better behavioral specifications rather than reward hacking.

sections.heading: Grounding: execution feedback vs. LLM judgment.
sections.text: Replacing execution-based feedback with LLM-as-a-judge scoring causes a large performance drop from 93.2 to 73.6, i.e., a decrease of 19.6 percentage points. Self-assessment is exactly the corrupted-signal regime of Theorem 1 : the robustness of the loop to imperfect tests stems from grounding in execution, not from tolerance to arbitrary noise, and the execution signal cannot be substituted by model judgment.

sections.heading: Coverage: sparser generated test suites.
sections.text: Lowering the coverage threshold τ cov \tau_{\mathrm{cov}} from its default of 0.9 to 0.7 or 0.5 has only a very small effect on performance, with ϕ ¯ \bar{\phi} remaining above 92. At the more aggressive setting τ cov = 0.3 \tau_{\mathrm{cov}}=0.3 , performance decreases to 87.5, corresponding to an overall drop of 5.7 percentage points relative to the default configuration. Degradation is graceful rather than brittle: the loop does not depend on a complete test suite, only on an execution-grounded one.

sections.heading: Implication for recursive self-improvement.
sections.text: Execution grounding matters more than signal density. Thinning the execution signal degrades performance gracefully: even the sparsest test suite ( τ cov = 0.3 \tau_{\mathrm{cov}}{=}0.3 , 87.5) still outperforms the LLM judge (73.6) by 13.9 points. A sparse but execution-grounded signal is therefore a better optimization target than a dense judgment-based one. This points to a general principle: in recursive self-improvement, the agent may propose its own feedback signal, provided that signal is grounded in execution. It also explains why code is a privileged substrate for self-improvement. Code is executable, testable, and iterable by nature, so every attempt yields grounded feedback, such as failing assertions, type errors, and stack traces, which the agent can use as an improvement signal without any external supervision. sections.heading: Appendix F Prompt Templates
sections.text: All prompts in this appendix are reproduced verbatim from our implementation; they refer to the specification as “documentation”. The error-driven refinement process consists of two stages: diagnosis and prescription.

sections.heading: F.1 Stage 1: Diagnosis Prompt
sections.text: Diagnosis Prompt Template You are analyzing test failures to diagnose why an LLM failed to generate correct code. Entity Information: - Name: {entity_name} - Type: {entity_type} (function/class/method) - Current Documentation: {current_doc} Test Failures: The generated code failed the following tests: {error_messages} Task: Analyze the test failures and diagnose: 1. What went wrong? Identify the specific errors (type mismatches, incorrect outputs, missing logic, etc.) 2. Why did the LLM fail? What information is missing or ambiguous in the documentation that caused the LLM to misunderstand the requirements? 3. What knowledge gap exists? What does the LLM need to know to generate correct code? Output: Provide a concise diagnosis in the following format: - Error Type: [brief description] - Root Cause: [what the LLM misunderstood] - Missing Information: [what needs to be clarified]

sections.heading: F.2 Stage 2: Prescription Prompt
sections.text: Prescription Prompt Template You are refining documentation for a code entity based on a diagnosis of test failures. Entity Information: - Name: {entity_name} - Type: {entity_type} - Current Documentation: {current_doc} Diagnosis: {diagnosis_output} Task: Refine the documentation to address the diagnosed issues. The refined documentation should: 1. Directly address the identified knowledge gap 2. Clarify the ambiguous or missing information 3. Be precise enough for an LLM to generate correct code 4. Preserve all existing correct information Output: Provide only the refined documentation, without any explanation.

sections.heading: F.3 Code Generation Prompt
sections.text: Code Generation Prompt Template Generate Python code for all entities in this module based on their documentation. Module: {module_name} Documentation: {all_entity_documentation} Requirements: • Implement each entity exactly according to its documentation • Ensure all cross-entity calls are consistent • Do not add functionality not specified in the documentation Output: Provide the complete Python implementation for all entities, without any explanation or markdown.

sections.heading: F.4 Test Case Generation Prompt
sections.text: Test Case Generation Prompt Template You are generating test cases for a code entity. Each test case includes inputs, expected outputs, and a description of what is being tested. Entity Information: - Name: {entity_name} - Type: {entity_type} (function/class/method) - Signature: {signature} - Source Code: {source_code} Dependencies: The following entities are called by this entity: {dependency_signatures} Task: Generate diverse test cases that cover: 1. Normal cases: typical usage scenarios 2. Edge cases: boundary conditions, empty inputs, single elements 3. Corner cases: special values, type boundaries Requirements: • Each test case must include input, expected output, and description • The description should explain what aspect of the entity is being tested • Cover different code paths and branches • Include cases that test error handling if applicable Output Format: Provide test cases as a JSON list: [ { "input": {"args": [...], "kwargs": {...}}, "expected_output": ..., "description": "Tests that ..." }, ... ] Provide only the JSON list, without any explanation.

sections.heading: F.5 Iterative Refinement Prompt (Baseline)
sections.text: Iterative Refinement Prompt Template You are refining documentation for a code entity based on test failures. Entity Information: - Name: {entity_name} - Type: {entity_type} - Current Documentation: {current_doc} Test Failures: The generated code failed the following tests: {all_error_messages} Task: Refine the documentation to fix the issues revealed by the test failures. The refined documentation should enable an LLM to generate correct code. Output: Provide only the refined documentation, without any explanation. Note: Unlike SpecForge ’s two-stage diagnosis-prescription process, the iterative baseline conditions on all error messages simultaneously in a single refinement step, which can lead to the signal corruption phenomenon described in § 3.3 .

sections.heading: Static Methods.
sections.text: RepoAgent [ 10 ] : We use the official implementation with default hyperparameters. Documentation is generated in a single pass without test feedback. DocAgent [ 11 ] : We use the official implementation. Multi-agent collaboration generates documentation iteratively until convergence.

sections.heading: Commercial Agents.

sections.heading: Prompt Optimization Methods.
sections.text: We adapt two state-of-the-art prompt optimizers to our setting by treating the entire specification bundle 𝒟 = ( d 1 , … , d n ) \mathcal{D}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}) as a single optimizable prompt. GEPA [ 13 ] . We implement a DSPy module where the input is the module’s source code and the output is the complete specification bundle for all entities. The metric function evaluates each candidate by generating code from the specifications, executing the same LLM-generated test suite that SpecForge receives during search (§ J ; ground-truth tests are withheld from all methods), and returning both a scalar score (solve rate) and textual feedback (formatted error messages from failing tests). We run GEPA with auto="heavy" and set max_metric_calls=50 to match SpecForge’s budget B = 50 B=50 . Each metric call corresponds to one full spec → \to code → \to test evaluation cycle. ACE [ 14 ] . We implement ACE’s Generator-Reflector-Curator pipeline adapted for specification optimization. The Generator produces specifications from source code conditioned on the current playbook. The Reflector analyzes test failures to extract lessons (e.g., “entity X’s documentation lacks return type specification”). The Curator converts lessons into delta bullets appended to the playbook. Each iteration performs one full spec → \to code → \to test evaluation cycle against the same LLM-generated test suite used by SpecForge (§ J ); we run for 50 iterations to match SpecForge’s budget. Following the original implementation, we use execution feedback (test pass/fail + error messages) without ground-truth labels. Critically, both methods optimize the specification bundle monolithically—they cannot attribute failures to individual entities or reason about inter-entity dependencies. This design choice is intentional: it evaluates whether state-of-the-art prompt optimization can succeed without the structural decomposition that SpecForge introduces.

sections.heading: DocSearch.
sections.text: We use the official implementation [ 24 ] with its default hyperparameters, guided by the same LLM-generated test suite that SpecForge receives (§ J ) and evaluated on the same hidden ground-truth tests. All results are obtained on the version of DevEval+ used in this paper, which is a deliberately more challenging setup than the one in the original DocSearch paper, curated to stress-test SpecForge: modules are larger and more densely tested (12.4 entities per module and 3.1 tests per entity, vs. 11.4 and 2.8).

sections.heading: Appendix H DevEval+ Benchmark
sections.text: This appendix provides comprehensive details about the DevEval+ benchmark used for evaluation.

sections.heading: H.1 Overview
sections.text: DevEval+ is a curated benchmark for module-level code generation, designed to evaluate methods under complex dependency structures. The benchmark comprises 20 Python modules containing 247 entities (functions, classes, and methods) validated by 760 test cases . Modules are sourced from two origins: (1) DevEval [ 5 ] , an existing repository-level code generation benchmark, and (2) additional open-source GitHub repositories selected to increase domain diversity and structural complexity. Key statistics of the benchmark: • Average dependency depth : 4.2 levels • Maximum dependency depth : 10 levels • Average entities per module : 12.4 • Average tests per entity : 3.1

sections.text: Table 3 presents the complete list of modules in DevEval+ , including their source, domain, and structural statistics. Table 3 : Complete module list of DevEval+ . Source : D = DevEval, G = GitHub. Modules marked with † \dagger are included in the cross-language subset DevEval+-Java .
