sections.heading: Source Selection Criteria.
sections.text: We selected modules based on the following criteria: 1. Non-trivial dependencies : Modules must contain at least 3 levels of call depth to exhibit meaningful output coupling effects. 2. Testability : All entities must have well-defined input-output behavior amenable to automated testing. 3. Self-containment : Modules should minimize external dependencies beyond the Python standard library to ensure reproducible evaluation. 4. Domain diversity : We balanced modules across application domains to avoid benchmark-specific overfitting.

sections.heading: From DevEval.
sections.text: We selected 10 modules from DevEval [ 5 ] : arxiv_digest , hybrid_images , textcnn , chakin , geotext , hone , lice , particle-swarm-optimization , readtime , and stocktrends . These modules span diverse domains including NLP, image processing, finance, and optimization. DevEval modules provide high-quality, human-verified test cases. We retained the original test suites without modification.

sections.heading: From GitHub.
sections.text: To increase structural complexity and domain coverage, we collected 10 additional modules from open-source GitHub repositories: interpreter , croniter , peakutils , pyfaidx , lexer , schedule , patternpy , schema , parser , and streaming-indicators . The data collection process consists of two phases: repository selection and quality assurance. In the repository selection phase, we searched GitHub for Python repositories with permissive licenses (MIT, Apache 2.0, BSD) and non-trivial dependency structures (call graph depth ≥ 3 \geq 3 ). Crucially, we required candidates to include existing ground-truth test suites, as this ensures reliable evaluation without introducing annotation artifacts from manual test construction. In the quality assurance phase, two authors independently set up the environment for each candidate repository and executed its test suite to verify functionality. Following this sanity check, annotators reviewed each test case for correctness and quality, verifying that tests accurately capture intended behavior rather than implementation quirks. Repositories were included only with unanimous agreement on test suite quality.

sections.heading: H.4 Dependency Structure
sections.text: The benchmark exhibits significant structural complexity to induce meaningful output coupling effects. Across all 20 modules, the average dependency graph depth is 4.2 levels with a maximum of 10 levels. Approximately 39% of entities are leaf nodes (no callees), while 30% are root nodes (no callers). This structure ensures that refinements to callee specifications can propagate through multiple levels, creating the conditions necessary to observe and address the whack-a-mole phenomenon.

sections.heading: H.5 Test Suite Construction
sections.text: All test cases in DevEval+ are sourced from ground-truth test suites: DevEval modules include human-verified tests from the original benchmark, while GitHub modules contain tests from their respective repositories. We performed verification on top of the upstream tests, with lightweight harness adjustments (import-path fixes and fixture rewiring) to integrate them into our evaluation pipeline.

sections.heading: Quality Assurance.
sections.text: All test cases were validated through: 1. Execution verification : Every test passes on the reference implementation. 2. Correctness review : Two authors independently verified that tests capture intended behavior rather than implementation quirks. 3. Independence check : Tests for entity e i e_{i} do not depend on implementation details of entities other than e i e_{i} ’s direct callees.

sections.heading: H.6 Cross-Language Subset (DevEval+-Java)
sections.text: For cross-language transfer experiments (§ 4.5.1 ), we constructed DevEval+-Java by translating test harnesses for a 16-module subset (marked with † \dagger in Table 3 ). This subset contains 208 entities validated by 680 test cases.

sections.heading: Translation Process.
sections.text: 1. Test input preservation : Input values were preserved exactly, with Python data structures mapped to Java equivalents (e.g., list → \to ArrayList , dict → \to HashMap ). 2. Expected output adaptation : Outputs were adapted for Java type system while preserving semantic equivalence. 3. Harness rewriting : Test harness code was manually rewritten in JUnit 5 format. 4. Verification : Two authors independently verified semantic equivalence of translated tests.

sections.heading: Subset Selection.
sections.text: The 16 modules were selected by excluding 4 modules whose Python implementations depend on libraries without direct Java equivalents, with the remaining modules satisfying: • Balanced source distribution (7 from DevEval, 9 from GitHub) • Representative depth distribution (range: 3–10, mean: 4.3) • Domain diversity (no more than 2 modules per domain)

sections.heading: Appendix I New Feature Implementation Setup ( SWE-Dev )
sections.text: This section details the new feature implementation experiment of § 4.5.2 : how SWE-Dev tasks and their PRDs are constructed, what each condition receives, and what the comparison tests.

sections.heading: Task construction.
sections.text: Each SWE-Dev instance is built from an open-source PyPI package with an executable, developer-written test file [ 9 ] . The test file is run under a tracer to obtain the call tree of the source functions it triggers; target functions are selected from this tree, and their implementations are removed from the repository. Difficulty follows call-tree depth: easy instances have depth 1–2, and hard instances have depth ≥ 3 \geq 3 and typically require implementing five or more interdependent functions. The test file is the evaluation oracle.

sections.heading: How the PRD is generated.
sections.text: The PRD shipped with each instance is written by GPT-4o in two parts [ 9 ] . A module-level description is synthesized from the test file. A function-level description of each target is obtained by augmenting the target’s original docstring with implementation-level details, with the prompt conditioned on the full code of its file, including the target function itself. The PRD concatenates the module description with, for each target, its signature, the augmented docstring, and a list of related functions ( DEPENDENCIES ). The PRD is therefore derived from the tests and the reference implementation, and it describes only the functions to be implemented: existing functions that the targets call appear in the dependency list by name only, without any description of their behavior.

sections.heading: Conditions.
sections.text: All conditions receive the same stubbed package source, in which the target functions are removed, and are scored by Pass@1 on the instance’s test file following the SWE-Dev protocol. They differ only in the accompanying text: • PRD+Source : the full SWE-Dev PRD described above. • Spec+Source (RepoAgent, Claude Code ∗ , ACE, SpecForge ): the signature and original docstring of each target function, which state what the new feature must provide, together with the specifications of the existing codebase produced by the method.

sections.heading: Specification generation and masking.
sections.text: Each method generates specifications on the complete package, so that the codebase is executable, as it is in real development before a feature is added, and every entity has a reference behavior from which SpecForge can derive test oracles. Deleting the target functions from a complete module beforehand would leave the module unable to run, since the remaining code still references them, which would rule out execution-based optimization methods such as SpecForge . Before the implementation step, we remove the specifications of the target functions. No method observes the instance’s evaluation test file.

sections.heading: Additional results analysis.
sections.text: The two conditions trade task-specific information against codebase-level information. The PRD describes the target functions in detail but says nothing about the behavior of the existing code they build on; the Spec+Source conditions describe the target functions only minimally but describe the whole existing module. New features are rarely self-contained: SWE-Dev targets call into existing functions, constants, and exception types, and a correct implementation must use them exactly as they behave. For example, in the vulture configuration task, the PRD requires _check_input_config to validate values against DEFAULTS and to raise InputError , but never states which keys DEFAULTS contains or how InputError is constructed. We refer to this missing knowledge as the semantic gap of the PRD. The experiment therefore asks whether a better semantic understanding of the existing module lets an agent implement a high-quality feature from only the minimal information that defines it. Because the PRD condition receives strictly more target-specific information, derived from the reference implementation, the comparison is conservative for the Spec+Source conditions.

sections.heading: Appendix J Test Case Generation
sections.text: This appendix describes the LLM-based test case generation process used to guide SpecForge ’s search without access to ground-truth tests.

sections.heading: J.1 Overview
sections.text: SpecForge operates as a self-improving framework where the search is guided by LLM-generated test cases rather than ground-truth tests. This design choice reflects realistic deployment scenarios where comprehensive test suites may not exist. The key insight is that even imperfect tests provide valuable diagnostic signals—test failures reveal knowledge gaps in the specifications, enabling targeted refinement. The test generation process follows a generate-then-validate approach: 1. Test generation : The LLM generates complete test functions—including inputs, assertions, and error messages—based on entity signatures and reference source code. 2. Validation : Each generated test is executed on the reference implementation. Only tests that pass are retained; those that fail (due to incorrect assertions or invalid inputs) are discarded. Two additional filters are applied post-validation: (i) tests that reach the target entity only via transitive calls to other functions are discarded, ensuring each retained test directly exercises its target; and (ii) tests with identical normalized inputs and assertions are deduplicated. This ensures test correctness by construction: every retained test is consistent with the reference implementation and contributes a distinct diagnostic signal.

sections.heading: J.2 Coverage-Driven Test Generation
sections.text: For each entity e i e_{i} , we employ a coverage-driven generation strategy. The LLM generates test functions iteratively until branch coverage exceeds a target threshold τ cov \tau_{\text{cov}} . Each iteration prompts the LLM to generate tests covering: • Normal cases : Typical usage scenarios with common input values • Edge cases : Boundary conditions (empty inputs, single elements, maximum values) • Corner cases : Special values that exercise specific code paths • Uncovered branches : When coverage feedback is available, tests targeting uncovered code regions The generation loop terminates when (1) branch coverage reaches τ cov \tau_{\text{cov}} (primary criterion), or (2) the per-iteration branch coverage gain stays below a positive threshold ε \varepsilon for P P consecutive iterations (no-progress early-stop). The loop is bounded because (i) progress iterations (gain ≥ ε \geq\varepsilon ) number at most ⌊ 1 / ε ⌋ \lfloor 1/\varepsilon\rfloor , since branch coverage is bounded above by 1.0 1.0 and each contributes at least ε \varepsilon ; and (ii) no-progress iterations (gain < ε <\varepsilon ) cannot accumulate indefinitely because the P P -th consecutive one triggers the early-stop. The generation prompt (provided in Appendix F ) includes: • Entity signature and type information • Reference source code for understanding expected behavior • Dependency signatures to ensure consistency with callees • Coverage feedback as ( line number , source snippet ) (\text{line number},\text{source snippet}) pairs extracted from coverage.py ’s branch-coverage output, indicating which lines remain uncovered

sections.heading: J.3 Quality Considerations
sections.text: While the validation step ensures test correctness, LLM-generated tests may have quality limitations that motivate our diversified error batch sampling (§ 3.3 ).

sections.heading: Error Message Quality Variation.
sections.text: Since the LLM writes complete test functions, the diagnostic value of error messages depends entirely on how each assertion is written. Some tests include informative messages (e.g., assert result == [1,2,3], f"Expected [1,2,3] got {result}" ) that directly reveal the failure mode, while others use bare assertions (e.g., assert result == expected ) that produce only AssertionError with no actionable signal. This heterogeneity is inherent to LLM-generated tests and cannot be controlled a priori.

sections.heading: Input Quality Variation.
sections.text: Not all generated test inputs are equally informative. Some inputs may exercise redundant code paths, miss critical edge cases, or cluster around similar patterns. By conditioning refinements on different test subsets, diversified error batch sampling increases the probability of encountering informative failure signals.

sections.heading: External Dependencies.
sections.text: External dependencies (filesystem, network, time, randomness) are detected via static analysis of import statements and AST patterns; the LLM is then prompted to isolate them through pytest fixtures (mocks for filesystem and network calls, frozen-time wrappers for time-dependent code) so that test outcomes remain deterministic and reproducible across runs.

sections.heading: J.4 Hyperparameters
sections.text: We use the following hyperparameters for test generation: • LLM : GPT-4o (fixed across all experiments for consistency) • Temperature : τ = 0.7 \tau=0.7 for input diversity • Coverage threshold : τ cov = 90 % \tau_{\text{cov}}=90\% branch coverage • No-progress patience : P = 2 P=2 consecutive iterations within ε = 0.01 \varepsilon=0.01 coverage gain

sections.heading: Behavioral specifications as vertical knowledge.
sections.text: Behavioral specifications can be viewed as a form of vertical knowledge: repository-specific facts about what each program entity does, which are absent from a model’s weights and must be supplied to it at inference time. A broad line of work studies how such domain knowledge is acquired, structured, and used by LLMs. In cyber threat intelligence (CTI), LLMs have been used to construct knowledge graphs from unstructured threat reports [ 60 ] , retrieval-augmented LLMs have been benchmarked over heterogeneous CTI sources [ 61 ] , and CTI corpora have been organized into agent-native scaffolds for direct consumption by agents [ 62 ] . Related efforts parse hybrid system logs into structured templates [ 63 ] and translate natural language into first-order logic that symbolic reasoners can consume [ 64 ] , and documentation optimized as repository-specific playbooks for coding agents [ 24 ] brings this view to software. These works share the premise that knowledge should be represented in the form its consumer can use. They differ from SpecForge in how the representation is judged and improved: knowledge graphs, retrieval corpora, and parsers are typically constructed once and evaluated by extraction or answer accuracy, whereas SpecForge treats the knowledge artifact itself as the object of recursive improvement, judges it by the behavior it induces in the consuming agent, and revises it until that behavior is verified correct.

sections.heading: Appendix L Compute Resources Used
sections.text: All evaluations involving proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet), were conducted through the APIs. These calls were issued from standard desktop machines using CPU-only execution, with no reliance on local GPU hardware, which makes the approach easy to reproduce in widely available computing environments. For open-source models (e.g., Qwen), inference was run on a single node equipped with eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs (80 GB each). Experiments were executed sequentially on this node to maintain consistent and reproducible runtime conditions across different model families. Overall, this setup highlights the modest computational demands of our method and shows that our approach remains practical and scalable even in resource-constrained settings when hosted APIs are used.

sections.heading: Appendix M Use of LLMs
sections.text: In this work, large language models (LLMs) were primarily used for inference in the specification generation experiments. Specifically, they were employed to generate responses under different prompting and evaluation settings, which enabled us to assess the effectiveness of our method across a range of generation tasks and model families. In addition to their role in experimental inference, LLMs were also used as a writing assistant during manuscript preparation. In particular, they helped improve the clarity, fluency, and overall readability of the paper by polishing sentence-level expressions and refining the presentation of technical descriptions. All substantive technical content, experimental design, analysis, and conclusions were determined and verified by the authors.

sections.heading: Appendix N Limitations
sections.text: The recursion in SpecForge is over specifications, not over the improver: the search procedure itself is fixed, and the loop requires a reference implementation against which self-generated tests are validated. Our evaluation of the loop covers 20 Python modules; other languages appear only as a downstream target in the cross-language transfer experiment (§ 4.5.1 ).

sections.heading: Appendix O Broader Impact
sections.text: This work studies how a coding agent can improve the behavioral specifications in its harness: natural-language descriptions of program behavior that are written for code-generation models and verified by execution, in contrast to human-facing documentation. Its main potential benefit is to improve the reliability, controllability, and practical utility of LLM-based coding agents in tasks such as code synthesis, migration, translation, and feature development, thereby reducing iteration cost and improving software quality. At the same time, more effective autonomous coding systems may lower the barrier to producing software at scale, including in harmful settings. The self-improvement studied here is bounded by design: it changes neither model weights nor the search procedure, and every candidate revision is evaluated by execution against tests validated on the reference implementation. Our method does not remove the need for verification or human oversight; it operates entirely through test-based feedback and does not introduce capabilities beyond improving the behavioral precision of specifications for downstream code generation. We therefore view its societal implications as broadly aligned with those of existing LLM-based software engineering systems, with the main positive contribution being better-structured, more evaluable interaction between codebases and generative models.

sections.heading: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.text: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. • The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. • The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. • It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We discuss the limitations of the work in the Limitations section (Appendix N ) and the sensitivity analysis. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. • The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper. • The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. • The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. • The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. • The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. • If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. • While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All theoretical results state assumptions explicitly and provide complete proofs in the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. • All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced. • All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. • The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition. • Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. • Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide detailed experimental information in the appendix and release source code that can reproduce the reported results. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. • If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. • Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. • While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We release code and data at https://github.com/ccsnow127/SpecForge . Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. • Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark). • The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines ( https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy ) for more details. • The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. • The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. • At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). • Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We specify all training and test details in the experiments section and the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. • The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We repeated experiments across multiple random seeds and report mean and standard deviation in the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. • The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). • The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.) • The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). • It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. • It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. • For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). • If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We provide sufficient information on computational resources in the appendix. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. • The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. • The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. • The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines ? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The research conducted in the paper conforms, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. • If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics. • The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We discuss potential positive and negative societal impacts in the Broader Impact section. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. • If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. • Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. • The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. • The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. • If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper poses no such risks. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. • Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. • Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. • We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We properly credit the creators of all assets used in the paper and respect the licenses and terms of use. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. • The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. • The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL. • The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. • For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. • If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset. • For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. • If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We document the new benchmark in the appendix and release it under permissive licenses. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. • Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. • The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. • At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: Our paper does not involve crowdsourcing or research with human subjects. Guidelines: • The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. • Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. • According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Affiliation: NEC Laboratories America Email: weicheng@nec-labs.com Abstract Coding agents based on frozen language models can improve their performance by refining the external context they rely on, without updating model weights. In this paper, we study recursive self-improvement (RSI) through behavioral specifications : natural-language code documentation that describes the behavior of program entities and guides agents in generating correct code. We formulate a self-improvement loop in which an agent generates code from its current specifications, evaluates the generated code using execution-verified tests, and refines the specifications based on observed failures. The improved specifications then guide subsequent code generation, allowing the agent to progressively improve its understanding of the codebase. However, recursive refinement is challenging because program entities are interdependent. Improving the specification of one entity can inadvertently degrade the correctness of others, a phenomenon we call output coupling . This creates a whack-a-mole effect in which local improvements cause regressions elsewhere, preventing consistent progress. We introduce SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework that addresses this challenge through three mechanisms: (i) Pareto-guided state selection preserves complementary specification states and prevents premature commitment; (ii) dependency-constrained entity selection prioritizes callee-before-caller refinement; and (iii) error-diversified expansion explores multiple refinements using different subsets of test failures. On DevEval+ , SpecForge achieves the best performance across five backbone models, including a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and a 5.7-percentage-point average improvement over the strongest baseline. The improved specifications also make the agent better at tasks outside the loop: they transfer to cross-language translation and to new-feature implementation, where they outperform the benchmark-provided requirement documents. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ccsnow127/SpecForge . 1 Introduction Large language models are increasingly used as autonomous coding agents. Systems such as Cursor [ 1 ] , Codex [ 2 ] , and Claude Code [ 3 ] can generate code, implement new features, and modify existing software with limited human intervention. Their effectiveness, however, depends heavily on how well they understand the behavior of the codebase they work with. This understanding is essential for tasks such as repository-level code generation [ 4 , 5 ] , legacy system migration [ 6 ] , cross-language reimplementation [ 7 , 8 ] , and new-feature implementation [ 9 ] . One way to provide such understanding is through behavioral specifications : natural-language code documentation that describes what individual program entities (e.g., functions, classes, and methods) do, including their inputs, outputs, and important behavioral constraints. Unlike traditional documentation intended primarily for human readers, these specifications serve as actionable knowledge that coding agents can use to generate and modify code. Importantly, because specifications are expressed in natural language, agents can also revise them based on feedback, creating an opportunity for self-improvement without changing the underlying language model. This motivates specification-mediated recursive self-improvement (RSI) , in which a coding agent iteratively improves its own behavioral specifications using feedback from code generation and execution, without modifying the underlying model weights. Starting from initial specifications, the agent generates code conditioned on these specifications alone and evaluates the generated implementations through unit tests. Test failures reveal missing or ambiguous behavioral information, which the agent uses to refine the specifications. The refined specifications then guide the next round of code generation, forming a recursive self-improvement loop. In our setting, the tests are automatically generated from the reference implementation and validated through execution, retaining only tests that pass. This provides reliable, execution-grounded feedback without requiring human annotations. Importantly, the objective is not to improve the reconstructed code itself, but to produce more accurate behavioral specifications. Their quality is measured not by readability or similarity to human-written documentation [ 10 , 11 ] , but by whether an agent can reconstruct behaviorally correct code from them. The resulting specifications capture reusable knowledge of the existing codebase, which can support downstream tasks such as cross-language translation and new-feature implementation, even when no reference implementation of the desired output is available. Despite its promise, specification-based RSI faces a fundamental challenge: program entities are not independent . Existing language-space optimization methods, such as MIPROv2 [ 12 ] , GEPA [ 13 ] , and ACE [ 14 ] , demonstrate that language models can improve their own context through iterative refinement and feedback [ 15 , 16 ] . However, directly applying this approach to behavioral specifications is difficult because changes to one entity can affect the behavior of others. We refer to this phenomenon as output coupling . It arises in two ways. First, dependency coupling occurs when the correctness of a caller depends on the behavior of its callees. Refining a caller before its callees are correctly specified can therefore produce misleading feedback. Second, generation coupling occurs because a coding model may condition on the entire specification bundle, so modifying one specification can change how other entities are generated, even without direct dependencies. Consequently, an update that fixes one entity may break another, creating a whack-a-mole effect: improvements are repeatedly undone by subsequent refinements, and the optimization process may oscillate rather than converge. For recursive self-improvement to be effective, it must therefore address three requirements: preserving previous progress, respecting dependencies between entities, and handling noisy or incomplete feedback during refinement. To address these challenges, we propose SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework for recursive self-improvement through behavioral specifications. Instead of following a single sequence of specification revisions, SpecForge explores multiple candidate specification states through three complementary mechanisms: ❶ Where to search: Pareto-guided state selection maintains an archive of non-dominated specification states with complementary strengths across program entities. This preserves alternative refinement paths and prevents premature commitment to a single solution. ❷ What to refine: Dependency-constrained entity selection uses the program’s call graph to restrict refinement to entities whose callees have already been resolved. A discounted-UCB bandit then adaptively allocates the refinement budget among eligible entities. ❸ How to refine: Error-diversified expansion generates multiple refinement candidates from different subsets of failing tests, allowing the search to explore alternative explanations for observed failures and reducing sensitivity to noisy feedback. Together, these mechanisms mitigate refinement interference and enable improvements to accumulate across recursive iterations. We evaluate SpecForge on DevEval+ , where behavioral specification quality is measured by the correctness of code reconstructed from the generated specifications. Across five backbone language models, SpecForge consistently outperforms strong documentation, prompt-optimization, and coding-agent baselines. In particular, it achieves a 94.9% solve rate with Claude-4.5-Sonnet and improves over the strongest baseline by 5.7 percentage points on average. We further evaluate whether the optimized specifications remain useful beyond the original code-generation task. Results on cross-language translation and new-feature implementation show that these specifications provide reusable behavioral knowledge that improves coding-agent performance in different software engineering settings. These findings suggest that refining behavioral specifications provides a practical approach to recursive self-improvement for coding agents, without requiring model weight updates. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We study specification-mediated recursive self-improvement for coding agents, in which behavioral specifications are iteratively improved through code generation and execution feedback. We identify output coupling as a central challenge that prevents naive iterative refinement from accumulating progress. • We introduce SpecForge , a dependency-guided multi-frontier tree search framework that combines Pareto-guided state selection, dependency-constrained entity selection, and error-diversified expansion to mitigate refinement interference and enable cumulative specification improvement. • We demonstrate that SpecForge consistently outperforms strong baselines on DevEval+ across five backbone models, and that its optimized specifications improve downstream cross-language translation and new-feature implementation. 2 Problem Formulation We study behavioral specification optimization : given source code, the goal is to produce, for every program entity, a natural-language specification from which a code-generation model can reconstruct a correct implementation without seeing the code. Rather than committing to a single rewrite trajectory, our solution preserves multiple competitive frontiers and expands them selectively. 3 Proposed Method We propose SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework for behavioral specification optimization. SpecForge instantiates the self-improvement loop of § 1 as search: each node is a specification state evaluated by executing the code generated from it, each edge is one self-revision driven by the failures of that code, and every revision starts from a state that earlier revisions produced. Figure 1 illustrates the search process: specification optimization proceeds not as a single rewrite trajectory, but as search over multiple partial solutions with different future refinement opportunities. By managing this search so that local refinements accumulate into stable global progress, SpecForge directly targets the whack-a-mole behavior induced by output coupling. State Representation. Self-improving LLM systems differ first in the substrate into which an improvement is written. Weight-space methods write into model parameters: the model is fine-tuned on data it generated itself [ 25 , 26 ] , on rewards derived from its own outputs [ 27 ] , or on rewards from a grounded environment [ 28 ] . The gain is amortized across tasks, but it cannot be read, diffed, or reverted. Context-space methods keep the weights frozen and write into the harness instead, through verbal self-refinement [ 29 , 30 , 16 ] , prompt search and textual gradients [ 15 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 12 , 13 ] , experience memory [ 14 ] , skill and tool synthesis [ 34 ] , or search over the whole scaffold [ 35 ] ; at the frontier, the procedure that performs the update is itself rewritten [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] . The improvement signal ranges from the model’s own judgment [ 39 , 40 ] to external verifiers such as tests [ 41 , 42 , 43 ] , compilers [ 44 , 45 ] , and environments [ 34 , 46 ] . SpecForge is a context-space method with an execution-based improvement signal and a fixed update procedure. The key difficulty in such a recursive self-improvement loop is that behavioral specifications are inherently coupled through the code generated from them, so that an improvement to one can cause a global regression and make the iterative process oscillate. Coding Agents. Coding is among the most rapidly advancing capabilities of LLM agents, in large part because code is executable, verifiable, and searchable: a candidate can be run, checked against tests, and improved by search. Agents such as Cursor, Codex, and Claude Code [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] now resolve issues and implement features across entire repositories [ 47 , 48 , 4 , 5 , 9 ] . The same property is carrying agents beyond conventional software, wherever the artifact can be expressed as a program or other interpretable text: games [ 49 ] , explanatory videos rendered from animation code [ 50 , 51 ] , 3D scenes written as Blender scripts [ 52 ] , and symbolic music [ 53 ] . SpecForge is complementary to these agents: it supplies behavioral specifications that a coding agent can condition on, which in our experiments improve cross-language translation and new-feature implementation (§ 4.5 ). Code Documentation. Documentation generation has evolved from template-based heuristics [ 54 , 55 , 56 ] through neural summarization [ 57 , 58 ] to modern LLM-based repository-level approaches. RepoAgent [ 10 ] extracts structural patterns from repositories to generate API references with hierarchical organization, while DocAgent [ 11 ] employs retrieval-augmented generation to produce context-aware explanations grounded in relevant code snippets. Both optimize for subjective quality metrics—clarity, completeness, and helpfulness—evaluated through human assessment or proxy metrics like BLEU scores against reference documentation. These approaches uniformly assume documentation serves human developers and measure quality through readability heuristics rather than downstream task performance. See Appendix K for further related work. 6 Conclusion We presented SpecForge , a multi-frontier tree search framework that makes specification-mediated self-improvement stable and compounding. A frozen coding agent improves by rewriting the behavioral specifications in its harness from the failures of the code it writes from them; unlike documentation written for human readers, a specification is judged only through the code it induces. Within this formulation, the central challenge is output coupling : because generated entities are behaviorally interdependent, locally beneficial refinements can trigger global regressions, rendering standard monolithic or sequential refinement unstable. SpecForge addresses this challenge through Pareto-guided frontier preservation, dependency-constrained entity selection, and error-diversified expansion, enabling stable progress under coupled search dynamics. Empirically, it consistently outperforms strong baselines on DevEval+ , exhibits superior search efficiency and robustness, and produces specifications that improve downstream performance in both cross-language translation and new-feature implementation, indicating that what the loop improves is reusable knowledge of the codebase rather than a fit to the tests that guided it.
